item.title: First Annual Conference on AI, Large Language Models, and the Social Sciences (LLMSS 2026)
item.description:
My paper “Scaling Reproducibility: An AI-Assisted Workflow for Large-Scale Replication and Reanalysis” has been accepted for presentation at the First Annual Conference on AI (Artificial Intelligence), Large Language Models, and the Social Sciences (LLMSS 2026), to be held 14–16 October 2026 at City University of Hong Kong. The paper appears in a thematic panel session, with a dedicated discussant and time for questions and discussion; the detailed panel programme and presentation slot will be circulated in September.

Talk: Scaling Reproducibility

Computational reproducibility — the ability to regenerate a study’s published numbers from its own code and data — is central to scientific credibility, yet verifying results at scale remains costly. The paper introduces an AI-assisted (artificial-intelligence-assisted) workflow for automated full-paper replication: it retrieves replication materials, reconstructs the computing environment, executes the original code, and matches the outputs to the point estimates reported in published regression tables.

Key findings from the study:

  • Universe definition. We define a universe of all empirical and quantitative papers from the three top political science journals (2010–2025) and measure stated data availability using automated extraction.
  • Replication at scale. For a stratified sample of 384 studies, we apply the workflow to conduct full-paper replication, totaling 3,382 empirical models.
  • Impact of mandates. Journal verification requirements, combined with data-archiving mandates, drive reproducibility: the full-paper reproducibility rate rises from 29.6% before DA-RT (Data Access and Research Transparency, a 2014 replication-transparency standard adopted across political science journals) adoption to 79.8% after, and — conditional on accessible replication packages — 94.4% of papers are fully reproducible (237 of 251).
  • Instrumental-variable diagnostics. As a secondary application, we apply standardized instrumental-variable (IV, a method for estimating causal effects using an external source of variation) diagnostics to 92 studies (215 specifications), illustrating how automated execution enables systematic reanalysis across heterogeneous empirical settings.

About the conference

LLMSS 2026 is organised by City University of Hong Kong’s Computational Social Sciences Lab, the University of Oxford’s Nuffield College Talking to Machines Initiative, and Peking University’s Analytics Lab for Global Risk Politics, with support from the European Political Science Association. Keynote speakers include Issa Dahabreh (Harvard University), Scott Hale (Oxford Internet Institute), Meng Tianguang (Tsinghua University), and Jonathan Zhu (City University of Hong Kong).

A day of pre-conference hands-on workshops (Tuesday, 13 October) covers topics such as AI (Artificial Intelligence) public-opinion polling, digital twins, the Silicon Jury, and prediction-powered inference. Accepted papers will be included in the open-access conference proceedings.

item.title: AI + Social Science Workshop
item.description:
I joined the tenth Luojia EMS Frontier Methods Bootcamp & AI + Social Science Workshop to exchange ideas on how generative AI reshapes empirical research in the social sciences. Hosted by the School of Economics and Management at Wuhan University, the workshop convened Raymond Duch, Lijia Wei, Lian Xue, Peiran Jiao, and other colleagues for a full day of methodological training and research dialogue.

Session highlights

  • 08:30-10:00 - Frontier methods overview. Raymond Duch outlined how LLMs can act as experimental subjects, pollsters, and market analysts, followed by Lijia Wei’s evidence on the Matching-LLM framework for forecasting public opinion.
  • 10:20-11:50 - Research methods training. Lian Xue discussed belief updating with medical AI explanations, and Peiran Jiao linked employee voice data from Glassdoor to firm valuation models.
  • 11:50-12:35 - My presentation. I presented Predictive Power, Bias, and Trust: Evaluating LLM-Driven Screening in FinTech Lending, showing how model governance and human oversight mitigate screening bias.
  • 14:00-16:00 - Roundtable discussion. Speakers stayed on for a closed-door session to trade implementation lessons on building trustworthy AI workflows for social-science data.

These conversations fed directly into my ongoing AIECON collaborations on data-centric AI, regulation, and human-centered evaluation of large language models.
